messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Hopelessness: I have no future, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo is a 24-year-old Latino man who came to treatment several years after a combat deployment, now living alone and working as a financial analyst in a downtown office. He described the defining event in fragments that were strikingly sharp in detail even as he struggled to place them in the right order. He could tell you the exact color of the dust hanging in the air, the metallic taste in his mouth, the weight of his gear pressing into his shoulders, and the sight of a fellow service member dropping in an open stretch of ground with nowhere to hide. But when he tried to tell the story from beginning to end, he would stop, correct himself, and start again. One image would break through suddenly—the exposed road, the sound of shouting, a body on the ground—and then vanish before he could connect it to what came just before or after. What remained most fixed for him was the unbearable clarity of being out in the open, visible and vulnerable, and the fact that someone from his unit did not come home.

In the months after he returned to the United States, Mateo found that reminders of the person he had lost were intolerable. He did not keep mementos, avoided photos, and quickly shut down anything that brought up death, memorials, or conversations about who had been killed. If family members asked about his deployment, he would give a flat answer and redirect the conversation. Friends learned not to press him. Being single suited him in this narrow sense; there was no partner at home asking why he woke quiet and tense or why certain subjects made him leave the room. He had come to believe that talking about what happened would force him back into moments he could not control, and he lived as if silence were the only reliable way to get through a day.

His work environment gave him regular encounters with the kinds of spaces he had begun to dread. As a financial analyst, he worked in a glass-heavy office with broad floors, open sightlines, and conference rooms that made him feel exposed. Crossing the lobby or standing in the center of a large meeting room could bring on an immediate sense of vulnerability, as if too much of him were visible and there was nowhere protected to stand. He began choosing routes that kept him close to walls, arriving early so he could take a seat at the edge of the room, and avoiding rooftop work events or outdoor lunches with colleagues. When team gatherings spilled into open plazas between office buildings, he often made an excuse and went back inside. Coworkers noticed that he was competent and serious but hard to know. Over time, this reserve contributed to his sense that he no longer belonged easily with other people.

What troubled Mateo as much as the memories themselves was what they seemed to say about him. He had come to believe that he had acted in ways that violated who he was supposed to be. He did not offer dramatic explanations; instead, he spoke with a quiet, fixed shame, as though some moral line had been crossed during combat and could not be uncrossed. He saw other young professionals making plans—graduate school, relationships, promotions—and felt cut off from that ordinary forward movement. “I have no future” was not something he said for effect. It reflected a genuine conviction that whatever life was supposed to open up into had ended for him over there. Around civilians, even other people his age, he felt permanently set apart. They talked about deadlines, dating, vacations; he carried images that arrived uninvited and a private certainty that they could never really understand him. In his mind, he was an outsider now, and not temporarily.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become narrow and lonely. He was functioning on paper—employed, punctual, productive—but his days were organized around avoiding reminders of loss, avoiding conversations about the deployment, and minimizing time in open or exposed spaces whenever he could. The memories remained exceptionally vivid, yet disjointed, capable of surfacing without warning in sharp flashes that left him briefly back inside the sensory world of combat. What finally brought him in was not one dramatic crisis but the accumulation of a life that felt increasingly sealed off. After leaving another office gathering because the open courtyard made him feel too exposed, and then spending the evening alone after ignoring calls from family he did not want to answer, he recognized how small his world had become. He came to treatment fearing that this estrangement was permanent—that he would always feel morally cut off, futureless, and apart from other people—but also hoping, cautiously, that he might find some way to live without arranging every day around what he cannot bear to remember or say.
